You are a blind semantic decoder of a natural-language crystal description. The user message is your only source of material-specific information. Understand the spatial narrative and produce a construction plan; do not guess missing independent numbers or look up a material. Return one JSON object only, without Markdown fences.
For sufficient information use:
{"status":"ok","space_group_number":integer,"hall_symbol":"Hall symbol stated in the text","lattice":[input_a,input_b,input_c,input_alpha,input_beta,input_gamma],"composition":{"Element":input_cell_atom_count},"orbits":[{"element":"Element","wyckoff":"multiplicity_and_letter","representative":[standard_fractional_x,standard_fractional_y,standard_fractional_z]}],"frame_transform":{"matrix":[[p11,p12,p13],[p21,p22,p23],[p31,p32,p33]],"origin_shift":[s1,s2,s3]},"round_digits":integer_or_null,"precision_corrections":[{"element":"Element","at":[input_fractional_x_before_correction,input_fractional_y_before_correction,input_fractional_z_before_correction],"delta":[fractional_dx,fractional_dy,fractional_dz]}]}
Lengths use angstroms, angles use degrees. The specified lattice and composition refer to the original input cell. Orbit representatives refer to the standard Hall coordinate frame. Copy the Hall symbol as a mathematical identifier rather than guessing a public-table integer number. Any equivalent representative of a declared orbit is allowed. Distinct independent orbits of the same element remain separate.
The geometry engine expands the public Hall symmetry orbits, applies q_input = inverse(P)(q_standard - s), selects images in the input cell, rounds fractional coordinates if round_digits is given, and applies precision corrections at their identified input-frame atom positions. If the text explicitly uses identical frames, supply identity P and zero shift. If no rounding is specified, use null. If no corrections are specified, use an empty array. All sites have full occupancy.
Numerical relations in the prose should be resolved into numbers in the plan. Do not silently replace the original geometry with an idealized one. For missing required information return {"status":"insufficient_information","reason":"..."}; for contradictory constraints return {"status":"conflict","reason":"..."}. Your input contains no source CIF or hidden data. Public crystallographic definitions are allowed; material-specific external retrieval is not.

The structure is described in the monoclinic space group Pm (No. 6, Hall symbol P -2y), which is a primitive monoclinic lattice with a mirror plane perpendicular to the b axis. The input cell is specified with lattice parameters a = 3.541356 Å, b = 9.692018 Å, c = 10.1735854 Å, α = 67.67380271°, β = 90.0°, and γ = 90.0°. This is a nonstandard monoclinic setting in which the unique axis is not the conventional b axis but rather the a axis, as indicated by the non-90° α angle. The input composition is Ta₁Nb₂Fe₁Se₁₀, totaling 14 atoms per unit cell.

The relationship between the input fractional coordinates q_input and the standard fractional coordinates q_standard is given by q_standard = P q_input + s, where the transformation matrix P is approximately [[0, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, -1]] (with negligible numerical noise on the order of 10⁻¹⁷ in the off-diagonal and diagonal entries) and the origin shift s is (0, 0, 0). This transformation effectively swaps the a and b axes and reverses the c axis direction, converting the nonstandard input cell into the conventional Pm setting. All atomic positions quoted below are given in the standard fractional coordinate frame.

The structure contains fourteen crystallographically independent atomic positions, each occupying a multiplicity-one Wyckoff site. Because the space group Pm has only a mirror plane at y = 0 (the 1a sites) and y = 1/2 (the 1b sites), every atom lies on one of these two mirror planes and is fully specified by its x and z fractional coordinates.

Tantalum occupies a single 1b site at (0.458900, 1/2, 0.081940). Niobium is distributed over two inequivalent sites: one Nb atom sits on the 1a site at (0.284475, 0, 0.372672), and a second Nb atom occupies the 1b site at (0.714270, 1/2, 0.638057). Iron occupies a single 1a site at (0.542811, 0, 0.896633).

The ten selenium atoms are distributed across ten distinct sites, five on the y = 0 mirror plane (1a sites) and five on the y = 1/2 mirror plane (1b sites). On the 1b plane, the Se atoms are located at (0.063235, 1/2, 0.249279), (0.488432, 1/2, 0.368551), (0.166475, 1/2, 0.500585), (0.723829, 1/2, 0.908606), and (0.355851, 1/2, 0.823465). On the 1a plane, the Se atoms are located at (0.937032, 0, 0.760016), (0.513753, 0, 0.645160), (0.828680, 0, 0.509221), (0.257951, 0, 0.091855), and (0.664306, 0, 0.153961).

All positional values are reported to six decimal places as rounded from the original data. No precision corrections were applied to any of the atomic positions, so the coordinates as given represent the original input geometry without adjustment toward any idealized symmetry constraints. The complete set of fourteen independent atomic positions, combined with the lattice parameters and the Pm space group symmetry, fully specifies the three-dimensional atomic arrangement of this TaNb₂FeSe₁₀ structure.
